newsitem.title: USA: Dollar hits new 4-year high vs yen as trade worries diminish.
newsitem.headline: Dollar hits new 4-year high vs yen as trade worries diminish.

text.p: The dollar surged to a four-year high against the yen on Monday, as fears the United States would use a weaker dollar to remedy trade imbalances with Japan subsided.

Although Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin urged Japan to guard against widening trade surpluses, his relatively benign rhetoric following a meeting with Japanese officials in Tokyo on Friday stoked dollar bulls, who had feared he would threaten to use a lower dollar as a weapon against rising Japanese exports.

While in Hanoi Monday on a six-day tour of Asia, Rubin said the recent strength of the dollar has been good for the U.S. economy. He declined to express a view on the dollar's future direction even though Japan reported that its February current account surplus -- the broadest measure of trade -- widened 15 percent to $6.92 billion in the previous 12 months.

"The lack of strong rhetoric from him is telling us that the U.S. won't use the dollar as a trade tool and there doesn't seem to be any problems with the Japanese trade surplus numbers that came out," said Dennis Pettit, foreign exchange manager at Long-Term Credit Bank of Japan.

"Last week those numbers would have caused the dollar to have sold off a little bit, but I think with the background of Rubin saying that the exchange rate won't be used as a trade tool, the market has been less responsive to the numbers."
A weaker dollar -- and stronger yen -- could make Japanese exports more expensive and U.S. products more attractive overseas.
The dollar vaulted to above 125 yen Monday, touching 125.81, its highest since January 1993. It settled at 125.58 yen, up from 124.30 late Friday.

The dollar also benefited from speculation that the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates another notch in May, which would make U.S. investments more alluring and draw capital from Japan and overseas, where yields are lower.

The notion that the Fed's recent rate hike was the first in what will turn out to be a series tightenings to ward off inflation gained ground on Friday, when U.S. employment data hinted that tight labour markets are starting to generate wage gains.

"It's keeping U.S./Japan rate spreads favourable and keeping the idea that Japanese investors will continue to look offshore for investments because returns at home are very low," said Bob Lynch, a senior currency analyst at MMS International.

The dollar was also lifted when the mark fell after British press reports that Bonn had softened its position that countries wishing to qualify for European Economic and Monetary Union must get government deficits down to no larger than 3.0 percent of economic output.

Finance Minister Theo Waigel denied reports in Monday's Financial Times and Guardian newspapers that he had relaxed his hardline stance on entry conditions for joining the single currency -- to be called the Euro -- planned for 1999. But the mark, currently Europe's preeminent currency, still weakened on worries that it would be supplanted by a weak Euro.
"You now have the possibility of a soft Euro, a soft EMU and spreads are wider now between U.S. and European rates," said Stephen Jury, chief dealer at Union Bank of Switzerland.
The dollar rose to 1.7125 marks from 1.6858 on Friday and to 1.4695 Swiss francs from 1.4425 Swiss. It fell to Canadian $1.3872 from C$1.3921 and the pound fell to $1.6278 from $1.6345.
